messages.subject: Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.subject_clean: Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am currently working on deriving the covariance matrix for the spatial field evaluated at observed locations S_obs based on a fitted SPDE model defined over a set of mesh nodes S_mesh. Reproducible code is provided below. Given the projector matrix, the observed values can be expressed as:

 Z_obs = A%*% Z_mesh

where Z_mesh denotes the latent spatial field at the mesh nodes. . Consequently, we have the distribution

  Z_obs ~ N(A%*% mu_mesh, A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T)
where mu_mesh= E[Z_mesh] and C_mesh = Cov(Z_mesh).

Using the Matérn covariance model implied by the SPDE formulation, the latent precision matrix Q_mesh=C_mesh^-1 can be obtained through the function inla.spde2.precision(). However, I am encountering challenges in computing the precision matrix or determinant of the projected covariance matrix A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T primarily due to rank deficiency stemming from the presence of zero-valued eigenvalues.

Would you happen to have any recommendations or best practices for dealing with this issue?

Thank you for your time!

Code:
library(INLA)
n=500
locations<-cbind(runif(n) , runif(n))
d=2

# Covariance Function Parameters using Equations (1), (2), (4), and (5) from Lindgren and Rue (2015)
# https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/download/v063i19/838
rho<-0.2
sigma2<-1
nu<-0.5
alpha<-nu + d/2
log_kappa <-log(8*nu)/2 - log(rho)
log_tau <-  0.5* log(gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)))- log(sqrt(sigma2))- nu *log_kappa
tau <- exp(log_tau)
kappa <- exp(log_kappa)

(8*nu)^(1/2)/kappa ; rho
gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)*kappa^(2*nu)*tau^2) ; sigma2

# Generate Mesh
mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(locations,
                   max.edge=c(.1), cutoff=0.01)

# Define the SPDE model (Matérn)
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = nu+1)
AMat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=locations)

# Obtain the precision matrix (Q) and covariance matrix (inv_Q) using specified parameter values
theta <- c(log_tau, log_kappa)  # log(tau), log(kappa)
Q <- inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta = theta)
inv_Q<-solve(Q)

# Compute observation-level covariance matrix and precision matrix
covMat <- AMat %*% inv_Q %*% t(AMat)
inv_covMat<-chol2inv(chol(covMat))
eigen(covMat)$values

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

there is a tool for this in `fmesher`;
When Q is the precision matrix and A1 and A2 are fm_basis() or inla.spde.make.A() output matrice,
  fm_covariance(Q, A1, A2)
computes the covariance between A1 * x and A2 * x.
If A2=A1=A, you can use the shorter form
  fm_covariance(Q, A)

The difference between that function and your code is that it doesn't evaluate the full inverse matrix solve(Q), but instead solves a linear system:

A1 %*% Matrix::solve(Q, Matrix::t(A2))

/Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.body_plain:
Hmmm,

I'd ask what you think you need that precision matrix for; as you note, it may be singular (e.g. if several locations lie within the same triangle) and also shouldn't be expected to have any sparsity structure; except for very specific special cases, the marginal observation precision matrix is fully dense.
The precision construction of the basis function representation of the spde models makes sense for the coefficients of the weights for the basis functions, but _not_ for the (joint marginal) distribution of the observations, whereas for those, the covariance matrix is well-defined (albeit potentially singular).

What actual question are you trying to answer?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Haavard,

Thanks for the response (and helpful code).  Apologies for my tardy reply -- hopefully there will be enough info here to jog your memory.

The code nearly does what I expect it to.  However, there are some situations where it gives unintuitive estimates.  The attached minor re-working of your example code is an illustrative example.  The problem is exacerbated when all the regression coefficients are positive.  If beta is negative (as in the example), then estimation proceeds as expected.

Some questions about the code:

* Why weight the fake zero observations with -1?  Why not '0' so that they don't contribute to the logl.  With -1, won't they (partially) cancel the contributions from the non-fake data?
* In the design matrix, the intercept term was filled with the simulation parameter.  Should this be 1 instead?  Note that Intercept.2 is assigned zero.
* The plots show that there might be a problem that the beta parameter is being applied to both otucomes.  I can't see how the model specification allows that though.

I also want to check: the covariates (x and xx in example) are the same for y1 and y2. This is not the case for my real application, nor are there the same amount of observations.  I presume that this is not a problem?

Thanks again,

Scott

> > The linear predictor for the second likelihood is
> > g(E(y2))=alpha2+gamma(X'beta), where alpha2 is another intercept, beta is as

> > I have made a little dummy data set (below) that highlights the problem.  Note

> >
> > Thanks in advance,
> >
> > Scott

> > #based on the example in
> > https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-INLAfeatures.html
> >
> > #model
> > #poisson model is exp( E( y1)) = alpha1 + b1*x1 + b2*x2 + b3*x3  #log link
> > #gaussian model is E( y2) = alpha2 + g * ( b1*x1 + b2*x2 + b3*x3) #identity
> > link
> >
> > library( INLA)
> >
> > set.seed( 747)
> >
> > #data attributes and covariates
> > N <- c(4000, 2000)
> > p <- 3

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the clarification and the quick response!

I’m working with a spatial dataset and wanted to evaluate the multivariate normal distribution using a covariance or precision matrix derived from a Matérn covariance function. I was curious whether I could use the SPDE approach to efficiently obtain the precision matrix (at the observed locations) and compute its determinant or eigenvalues. The main goal is to see if this would be more computationally efficient than fitting the full model without any approximations.

Thank you for your time.

On Mon, Jun 2, 2025 at 6:17 PM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hmmm,
>
> I'd ask what you think you need that precision matrix for; as you note, it may be singular (e.g. if several locations lie within the same triangle) and also shouldn't be expected to have any sparsity structure; except for very specific special cases, the marginal observation precision matrix is fully dense.
> The precision construction of the basis function representation of the spde models makes sense for the coefficients of the weights for the basis functions, but _not_ for the (joint marginal) distribution of the observations, whereas for those, the covariance matrix is well-defined (albeit potentially singular).
>
> What actual question are you trying to answer?
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 2 Jun 2025 at 23:50, Ben Lee <benl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you very much for the quick response as well as pointing me towards the fm_covariance() function.
> >
> > I am sorry, but I made a blunder in the original email. I am actually trying to compute the precision matrix, not the covariance,  between  A1 * x and A2 * x as well as the corresponding determinant. So I would need the inverse of A1 %*% Matrix::solve(Q, Matrix::t(A2))A1 %*% Matrix::solve(Q, Matrix::t(A2)).
> >
> > If the columns of A are not linearly independent,  then AQ^(-1)A^t would not be invertible as this example demonstrates. Should I just add a small nugget term to the diagonal to bypass this issue?
> >
> > On Monday, June 2, 2025 at 5:04:52 PM UTC-4 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > there is a tool for this in `fmesher`;
> > > When Q is the precision matrix and A1 and A2 are fm_basis() or inla.spde.make.A() output matrice,
> > >   fm_covariance(Q, A1, A2)
> > > computes the covariance between A1 * x and A2 * x.
> > > If A2=A1=A, you can use the shorter form
> > >   fm_covariance(Q, A)
> > >
> > > The difference between that function and your code is that it doesn't evaluate the full inverse matrix solve(Q), but instead solves a linear system:
> > >
> > > A1 %*% Matrix::solve(Q, Matrix::t(A2))
> > >
> > > /Finn
> > >
> > > On Mon, 2 Jun 2025 at 22:39, S B Lee <benl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hello,
> > > >
> > > > I am currently working on deriving the covariance matrix for the spatial field evaluated at observed locations S_obs based on a fitted SPDE model defined over a set of mesh nodes S_mesh. Reproducible code is provided below. Given the projector matrix, the observed values can be expressed as:
> > > >
> > > >  Z_obs = A%*% Z_mesh
> > > >
> > > > where Z_mesh denotes the latent spatial field at the mesh nodes. . Consequently, we have the distribution
> > > >
> > > >   Z_obs ~ N(A%*% mu_mesh, A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T)
> > > > where mu_mesh= E[Z_mesh] and C_mesh = Cov(Z_mesh).
> > > >
> > > > Using the Matérn covariance model implied by the SPDE formulation, the latent precision matrix Q_mesh=C_mesh^-1 can be obtained through the function inla.spde2.precision(). However, I am encountering challenges in computing the precision matrix or determinant of the projected covariance matrix A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T primarily due to rank deficiency stemming from the presence of zero-valued eigenvalues.
> > > >
> > > > Would you happen to have any recommendations or best practices for dealing with this issue?
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for your time!
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Code:
> > > > library(INLA)
> > > > n=500
> > > > locations<-cbind(runif(n) , runif(n))
> > > > d=2
> > > >
> > > > # Covariance Function Parameters using Equations (1), (2), (4), and (5) from Lindgren and Rue (2015)
> > > > # https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/download/v063i19/838
> > > > rho<-0.2
> > > > sigma2<-1
> > > > nu<-0.5
> > > > alpha<-nu + d/2
> > > > log_kappa <-log(8*nu)/2 - log(rho)
> > > > log_tau <-  0.5* log(gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)))- log(sqrt(sigma2))- nu *log_kappa
> > > > tau <- exp(log_tau)
> > > > kappa <- exp(log_kappa)
> > > >
> > > > (8*nu)^(1/2)/kappa ; rho
> > > > gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)*kappa^(2*nu)*tau^2) ; sigma2
> > > >
> > > > # Generate Mesh
> > > > mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(locations,
> > > >                    max.edge=c(.1), cutoff=0.01)
> > > >
> > > > # Define the SPDE model (Matérn)
> > > > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = nu+1)
> > > > AMat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=locations)
> > > >
> > > > # Obtain the precision matrix (Q) and covariance matrix (inv_Q) using specified parameter values
> > > > theta <- c(log_tau, log_kappa)  # log(tau), log(kappa)
> > > > Q <- inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta = theta)
> > > > inv_Q<-solve(Q)
> > > >
> > > > # Compute observation-level covariance matrix and precision matrix
> > > > covMat <- AMat %*% inv_Q %*% t(AMat)
> > > > inv_covMat<-chol2inv(chol(covMat))
> > > > eigen(covMat)$values
> > > >

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Obtain Precision/Covariance Matrix for Observed Locations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

I see. The problem is that the common intuition for how to compute things that is based on _starting_ with the covariance matrix isn't valid when what we have more direct access to is a sparse precision matrix. Nearly all expressions can be reformulated (usually using the "matrix inversion lemma") into expressions that do not actually involve the marginal observation covariance matrix. In short, when we work with sparse precision matrices, we rarely need to compute covariance matrices, and most quantities can be evaluated using a different set of standard computational expressions than those based on covariances.

For example, to evaluate the density for the observations, conditionally on the covariance parameters, one can rewrite the expression into functions of the field precision matrix Q_x, the conditional observation precision Q_e (typically a diagonal matrix) and the data-conditional precision for the field, Q_{x|y}, which is equal to Q_x +A' Q_e A, when A is the observation matrix (from fm_basis() or inla.spde.make.A()). The details can be seen in Section 3.1 of my notes on how to compute with Gaussian Markov random fields (a condensation of the relevant methods from the Rue&Held 2005 book on Gaussian Markov Random Fields) available at https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/cuso2019/gmrf.pdf

One of the few cases where we might explicitly want to have access to elements of the covariance matrix for y, S_y = Q_y^{-1}  is to access the pointwise marginal variances at the mesh nodes.
These can be computed by selected/partial inversion of Q_x, plus the noise variances;
  y_var = diag(inla.qinv(Q_x)) + diag(inla.qinv(Q_e))
Approximate variance evaluation can then be done with A %*% y_var, or (A %*% y_var^0.5)^2.
As long as A' A has non-sparsity that's contained in the sparsity of Q_x, the variances of A %*% x can also be obtained using tricks with the partial inverses; some of that is also written in the gmrf.pdf document.

To specifically answer your last question: It is possible to construct the mesh so it includes specific locations of interest (but this isn't always a numerically beneficial approach), but
you can _not_ obtain the joint precision matrix for _just_ those points by removing the other rows and columns from the matrix; doing that would only give you the _conditional_ precision matrix, i.e. the inverse of the _conditional_ covariance matrix, given all the other points. This can be seen either from the matrix inversion lemma or from block matrix inversion calculations;

If the covariance is
  S = [S_{AA}, S_{AB}; S_{BA}, S_{BB}]
and the precision is
  Q = [Q_{AA}, Q_{AB}; Q_{BA}, Q_{BB}],
then
  Q_{BB}^{-1} = S_{BB} - S_{BA} S_{AA}^{-1} S_{AB},
which is the conditional covariance of block B, given block A.
Conversely, the _marginal_ precision matrix for block B is
  S_{BB}^{-1} = Q_{BB} - Q_{BA} Q_{AA}^{-1} Q_{AB},
but there are few cases where calculating this is useful.

Finn

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

My apologies for the late response here. Thank you very much for the detailed and thoughtful comments and suggestions!

This is very promising for my project, and I will look into the details provided in your notes. Since we are able to compute Q_x, Q_{x|y} and Q_e easily, this would help with getting through the computational bottleneck. I also appreciate your feedback on my suggestion of using the locations as mesh nodes.

Again, thank you very much!

best,
Ben

On Tue, Jun 3, 2025 at 3:27 PM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Ben,
>
> I see. The problem is that the common intuition for how to compute things that is based on _starting_ with the covariance matrix isn't valid when what we have more direct access to is a sparse precision matrix. Nearly all expressions can be reformulated (usually using the "matrix inversion lemma") into expressions that do not actually involve the marginal observation covariance matrix. In short, when we work with sparse precision matrices, we rarely need to compute covariance matrices, and most quantities can be evaluated using a different set of standard computational expressions than those based on covariances.
>
> For example, to evaluate the density for the observations, conditionally on the covariance parameters, one can rewrite the expression into functions of the field precision matrix Q_x, the conditional observation precision Q_e (typically a diagonal matrix) and the data-conditional precision for the field, Q_{x|y}, which is equal to Q_x +A' Q_e A, when A is the observation matrix (from fm_basis() or inla.spde.make.A()). The details can be seen in Section 3.1 of my notes on how to compute with Gaussian Markov random fields (a condensation of the relevant methods from the Rue&Held 2005 book on Gaussian Markov Random Fields) available at https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/cuso2019/gmrf.pdf
>
> One of the few cases where we might explicitly want to have access to elements of the covariance matrix for y, S_y = Q_y^{-1}  is to access the pointwise marginal variances at the mesh nodes.
> These can be computed by selected/partial inversion of Q_x, plus the noise variances;
>   y_var = diag(inla.qinv(Q_x)) + diag(inla.qinv(Q_e))
> Approximate variance evaluation can then be done with A %*% y_var, or (A %*% y_var^0.5)^2.
> As long as A' A has non-sparsity that's contained in the sparsity of Q_x, the variances of A %*% x can also be obtained using tricks with the partial inverses; some of that is also written in the gmrf.pdf document.
>
> To specifically answer your last question: It is possible to construct the mesh so it includes specific locations of interest (but this isn't always a numerically beneficial approach), but
> you can _not_ obtain the joint precision matrix for _just_ those points by removing the other rows and columns from the matrix; doing that would only give you the _conditional_ precision matrix, i.e. the inverse of the _conditional_ covariance matrix, given all the other points. This can be seen either from the matrix inversion lemma or from block matrix inversion calculations;
>
> If the covariance is
>   S = [S_{AA}, S_{AB}; S_{BA}, S_{BB}]
> and the precision is
>   Q = [Q_{AA}, Q_{AB}; Q_{BA}, Q_{BB}],
> then
>   Q_{BB}^{-1} = S_{BB} - S_{BA} S_{AA}^{-1} S_{AB},
> which is the conditional covariance of block B, given block A.
> Conversely, the _marginal_ precision matrix for block B is
>   S_{BB}^{-1} = Q_{BB} - Q_{BA} Q_{AA}^{-1} Q_{AB},
> but there are few cases where calculating this is useful.
>
> Finn
>
> On Tue, 3 Jun 2025 at 20:45, Ben Lee <benl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > My apologies for the double message, but I had one other thought.
> >
> > If I we were to build a mesh such that the mesh consists of only the observed locations, we could use the  Q precision matrix directly in evaluating the multivariate normal distribution. Then we would not have to worry about the singularity issue as previously mentioned. That being said, is it possible to generate a mesh where the mesh nodes are the locations themselves? If there are additional mesh vertices, in addition to the observation locations, I could just remove the corresponding rows in the resulting Q matrix.
> >

> > > Thank you for the clarification and the quick response!
> > >
> > > I’m working with a spatial dataset and wanted to evaluate the multivariate normal distribution using a covariance or precision matrix derived from a Matérn covariance function. I was curious whether I could use the SPDE approach to efficiently obtain the precision matrix (at the observed locations) and compute its determinant or eigenvalues. The main goal is to see if this would be more computationally efficient than fitting the full model without any approximations.
> > >
> > > Thank you for your time.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mon, Jun 2, 2025 at 6:17 PM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hmmm,
> > > >
> > > > I'd ask what you think you need that precision matrix for; as you note, it may be singular (e.g. if several locations lie within the same triangle) and also shouldn't be expected to have any sparsity structure; except for very specific special cases, the marginal observation precision matrix is fully dense.
> > > > The precision construction of the basis function representation of the spde models makes sense for the coefficients of the weights for the basis functions, but _not_ for the (joint marginal) distribution of the observations, whereas for those, the covariance matrix is well-defined (albeit potentially singular).
> > > >

> > > > >

> > > > > > When Q is the precision matrix and A1 and A2 are fm_basis() or inla.spde.make.A() output matrice,

> > > > > > computes the covariance between A1 * x and A2 * x.
> > > > > > If A2=A1=A, you can use the shorter form

> > > > > > > Hello,

> > > > > > > I am currently working on deriving the covariance matrix for the spatial field evaluated at observed locations S_obs based on a fitted SPDE model defined over a set of mesh nodes S_mesh. Reproducible code is provided below. Given the projector matrix, the observed values can be expressed as:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >  Z_obs = A%*% Z_mesh
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > where Z_mesh denotes the latent spatial field at the mesh nodes. . Consequently, we have the distribution
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >   Z_obs ~ N(A%*% mu_mesh, A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T)
> > > > > > > where mu_mesh= E[Z_mesh] and C_mesh = Cov(Z_mesh).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Using the Matérn covariance model implied by the SPDE formulation, the latent precision matrix Q_mesh=C_mesh^-1 can be obtained through the function inla.spde2.precision(). However, I am encountering challenges in computing the precision matrix or determinant of the projected covariance matrix A%*%C_mesh%*%A^T primarily due to rank deficiency stemming from the presence of zero-valued eigenvalues.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Would you happen to have any recommendations or best practices for dealing with this issue?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thank you for your time!
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Code:
> > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > > n=500
> > > > > > > locations<-cbind(runif(n) , runif(n))
> > > > > > > d=2
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # Covariance Function Parameters using Equations (1), (2), (4), and (5) from Lindgren and Rue (2015)
> > > > > > > # https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/download/v063i19/838
> > > > > > > rho<-0.2
> > > > > > > sigma2<-1
> > > > > > > nu<-0.5
> > > > > > > alpha<-nu + d/2
> > > > > > > log_kappa <-log(8*nu)/2 - log(rho)
> > > > > > > log_tau <-  0.5* log(gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)))- log(sqrt(sigma2))- nu *log_kappa
> > > > > > > tau <- exp(log_tau)
> > > > > > > kappa <- exp(log_kappa)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > (8*nu)^(1/2)/kappa ; rho
> > > > > > > gamma(nu)/(gamma(alpha)*(4*pi)^(d/2)*kappa^(2*nu)*tau^2) ; sigma2
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # Generate Mesh
> > > > > > > mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(locations,
> > > > > > >                    max.edge=c(.1), cutoff=0.01)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # Define the SPDE model (Matérn)
> > > > > > > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = nu+1)
> > > > > > > AMat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=locations)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # Obtain the precision matrix (Q) and covariance matrix (inv_Q) using specified parameter values
> > > > > > > theta <- c(log_tau, log_kappa)  # log(tau), log(kappa)
> > > > > > > Q <- inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta = theta)
> > > > > > > inv_Q<-solve(Q)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # Compute observation-level covariance matrix and precision matrix

messages.subject_clean: Question About Shared Random Effects and the copy Feature
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question regarding shared effects in my model. My formula is as follows:

fomula = ... + f(r.Y, model="iid",  hyper = list(theta = list(initial=log(L.Y),fixed=TRUE))) + f(b.Y, copy="r.Y", hyper = list(beta = list(initial = tau, fixed = TRUE))).

In this setup, Y appears in both Model 1 and Model 2, and they are meant to share the same random effect. I have Y in model 1 and tau*Y in model 2. I expected r.Y and b.Y to have the same values. However, I noticed that the estimates of r.Y and b.Y differ.

I came across the explanation that "the main difference between the copy and replicate features is that with the copy effect, the values of the random effects are the same, but copied effects can be scaled by a parameter." I’m wondering if the difference in estimates is due to b.Y being scaled, and if so, what parameter is responsible for this scaling?

Additionally, which of the two—r.Y or b.Y—should be considered the true estimate of Y?

Thank you for your help.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was trying to construct the precision matrix using with inla.spde2.precision(), but I got two different answers. The first approach is to directly pass the parameter theta=(log(tau), log(kappa)) to get the precision matrix; the second approach is to pass theta=(0, log(kappa)), and then multiple the resulting precision matrix by tau. According to the equation on Page 4 of Lindgren and Rue (2015, Bayesian modeling with R-INLA), I should get the same precision matrix. However, the following test indicates that they are quite different. Am I missing something here? Thank you very much for any suggestions.

set.seed(123)

#--- Set up 2D grid
n1 <- 15
n2 <- 15
n <- n1 * n2
coords <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = n1),
                                y = seq(0, 1, length.out = n2)))
# Construct SPDE-based GMRF
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc      = coords,
                     cutoff   = 0.05,          # drop duplicates
                     max.edge = c(0.05, 0.1),  # inner / outer edge length
                     offset   = c(0.08, 0.1))  # extends mesh beyond data
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 2)  # nu=alpha - d/2
log_tau = log(2)
log_kappa = log(0.5)

# the precision matrix Q = tau^2 * Q_0, where Q_0=kappa^4 C + 2*kappa^2 G_1 + G_2
Q1 = inla.spde2.precision(spde, c(log_tau,log_kappa))
Q0 = inla.spde2.precision(spde, c(0,log_kappa))
Q2 = exp(log_tau) * Q0

norm(Q1-Q2,"F")

Thanks,
Pulong M

Hello,

I am reaching out to seek clarification on how the "bym2" function in INLA handles adjacency matrices when dealing with multiple records per spatial unit, such as repeated measurements over time or replicates due to a third factor.

Specifically, I want to ensure that the spatial adjacency matrix is correctly aligned with the order of spatial units in my dataset. I have attempted to build spatio-temporal models with and without replicates, but the fitted values do not seem to make sense, leading me to suspect that there might be an issue with how the adjacency matrix is being constructed.

To illustrate my concerns, I have attached a simulation that includes the code I use to fit the INLA model, along with the options I have specified. I would appreciate it if you could review this code and provide guidance on whether there are any potential issues with how I am building the model.

My primary concern is whether the adjacency matrix automatically recognizes the correct row for each spatial unit based on the index. I have provided two examples: a simple one with repeated records over time and a second one with a replicated factor that I would like to use within the random effect.

It's worth noting that I do not have complete information for all locations and have discarded some due to missing covariates. However, I have taken care to only consider the locations included in the model fitting and prediction, and I have built the graph accordingly.

I would be grateful for any clarification or guidance you can provide on how INLA's "bym2" function handles adjacency matrices in these scenarios. Please let me know if you require any additional information or context.

Thank you for your time and assistance.

Best regards

               "INLA", "tsModel", "splines","dlnm",
               "sf","tmap","basemaps","terra", "sp", "spdep", "pROC")

      install.packages("INLA", repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"), dep = TRUE)
    } else {
      install.packages(lib)
    }
  }
  library(lib, character.only = TRUE)
}

# Get all nuts code
nuts3<-gisco_get_nuts(nuts_level = 3,year=2021, epsg = 3035)

# Create a dataframe with all combinations of nuts IDs, months and years
df <- expand.grid(
  nuts_id = nuts3$NUTS_ID,
  month = 1:12,
  year = 2010:2023,
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS=FALSE
)

# Simulate Y outcome variable following a Poisson distribution
df$Y <- rpois(nrow(df), lambda = 30)

# Introduce some NA values for Y, but only for specific NUTS3
# Sample 100 unique nuts IDs
sample_nuts_ids <- sample(unique(nuts3$NUTS_ID), size = 100, replace = FALSE)

df$Y[df$nuts_id %in% sample_nuts_ids] <- NA # introduce NA values for specific NUTS3 regions

# Sample 3 unique nuts IDs to delete from the entire dataframe because you do not have records of covariates
sample_nuts_ids2 <- sample(unique(nuts3$NUTS_ID), size = 3, replace = FALSE)

# Exclude the ids from the original data
df <- df |>
  filter(!nuts_id %in% sample_nuts_ids2)

# Simulate TMEAN temperature in Kelvin (range: 257.1252 - 305.0120)

# Relocate some columns and create indexes for the graph  parameters
df<-df |>
  mutate(nuts_index=as.integer(factor(nuts_id)))|>
  relocate(nuts_index,.before=nuts_id) |> arrange(year,month,nuts_index)

# Create the graph

# Reorder the rows of nuts3 shapefile based on the order of NUTS_ID in data
nuts3 <- nuts3 |>  arrange(match(NUTS_ID, df$nuts_id))
head(nuts3)
head(df)

# Create the adj matrix

nb2INLA("Input/Data_model/graph", nuts3_nb)

g <- inla.read.graph(filename = "Input/Data_model/graph")

# Define the model formula

alpha <- 0.01
u <- 1

precision_prior <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(u, alpha)))

# Define the formula
formula <- Y ~ 1 +f(month, model = "rw1",cyclic = TRUE, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE, hyper = precision_prior) +
  f(nuts_index, model = "bym2",  graph = g, scale.model = TRUE, hyper = precision_prior) +log(TMEAN)

# Run the model

# Model to assess the relationships between the outcome and covariates

  # formula, data and model family

  control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive'),

  # items to compute
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, config = FALSE,
                         cpo = TRUE,return.marginals = TRUE),

  # fixed effects calibration

                       prec.intercept = 1, # precision 1
                       prec = 1), # weakly regularising on fixed effects (sd of 1)

  # save predicted values on response scale
  control.predictor = list(link = 1, compute = TRUE),

  # Verbose
  verbose = TRUE)

# Look at the predictions
df$fitted<-model$summary.fitted.values[,c("mean")]

head(df)

messages.subject: Issue Running inla() with mclapply on Cluster (Newton-Raphson Optimizer Did Not Converge)
messages.subject_clean: Issue Running inla() with mclapply on Cluster (Newton-Raphson Optimizer Did Not Converge)
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-INLA group,

I need your help to solve a problem I'm facing.

I'm encountering an issue when running the inla() function in parallel using mclapply (from the parallel package) on a computing cluster. More precisely, I'm using mclapply to run multiple inla() calls in parallel on different datasets. INLA itself also uses internal parallelism, so I reserved half the cores for that purpose. The same inla() model, runned serially (i.e., outside of mclapply), works fine on my local machine but seems to fail on the cluster (even if I execute it serially). However, this issue doesn't occur for all datasets. For some dataframes, the model fails both locally and on the cluster, while others work as expected.

Here are some details:
- Local setup: R version 4.4.3 (2024.12.1) on Windows
- Cluster setup: R version 4.5 (2025.05.0)
- INLA installation command (used both locally and on the cluster): install.packages("INLA", repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"), dep = TRUE)

I'm fitting a random error spatial joint model with a Poisson likelihood. The model formula is as follows:
formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept +
  f(sp.1, model = "bym2", scale.model = TRUE, graph = graph) +
  f(sp.2, copy = "sp.idx1", hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = TRUE))) +
  f(s.2, model = "iid")
inla(formula, data = df, family = "poisson",
     control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE), E = E,
     control.compute = list(config = TRUE, waic = TRUE), verbose = T)

When running this on the cluster using mclapply and allocating half of the available cores for INLA, I receive the following error:
GitId: b2abbedea53ff456149dbe37d7be47fdd0cfdf9f - Wed Dec 11 22:31:59 2024 +0300
Error:12 Reason: The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message: Condition ‘lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim’ is not TRUE
Line:1026 Function: GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern

I get the same error for certain datasets even when running locally. I’ve attached one such dataframe that reproduces the issue both on the cluster and on my machine.

Has anyone experienced similar behavior when using INLA with mclapply on a cluster? Could this be related to characteristics of specific datasets, or a version/environment mismatch? Any suggestions for debugging or resolving this would be greatly appreciated.

I could provide supplementary code and datasets if needed.

Thanks in advance!

Best regards,
Florine

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

there is no issues with the current example on my side. the package develop all
the time, so the default answer is always to upgrade.

I would suggest you try the following

- upgrade to R-4.5 everywhere. we only build for 4.5 hence you'll be stuck in
old versions without this

- use the testing version (just use 'testing' instead of 'stable'

	install.packages("INLA", repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA =

	"https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing"), dep = TRUE)

- with such small data, there is no need to use mclapply. you'll just make it
slower. or, you need to set number of threads the inla call to be small-ish,
like

	inla.setOption(num.threads="4:1")

and then you could try to mclapply beyond that

- the time of each run, is basically to compute the prior used in 'bym2', as the
inla-program runs in 0.15 seconds on my laptop.

- on the side-note, I do not understand your formula, well, this part

    f(sp.idx1, model = "bym2", graph = graph) +

    f(sp.idx2, copy = "sp.idx1", hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = T))) +

as idx1 is c(1:n,rep(NA,n)), and idx2 is c(rep(NA,n),1:n).  with these values
(and 'beta=1', fixed), then you might say the same using

    f(sp.idx1, model = "bym2", graph = graph) +

and set sp.idx1 = c(1:n, 1:n)  . it can be that this is just a snapshot of a
larger setup, but I just wanted to say

Best wishes
Havard

I'm not just running the model on a single dataset — I’m running it on over 30,000 varied datasets, so using mclapply() for parallelization is crucial to speed up computation by fitting several models at once.

Please let me know if there’s anything else I should try to resolve the cluster-side issue — I’m happy to test suggestions or provide additional details.

Best regards,
Florine

10,000's are ok. the 'copy' operator can only copy the whole model, but the

Hello,

In answer 22 (https://www.r-inla.org/faq#h.z4ecbkezo5tu) there is a link to a techincal report (in this tech-report <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fsites.google.com%2Fa%2Fr-inla.org%2Fwww%2Ffaq%2Fwaic_understand3.pdf%3Fattredirects%3D0&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AOvVaw2JH_cV898Iez_DoAx-DQkA>) that goes to a resource that does not exist.

This document seems to be the same as Gelman et al. 2014(DOI: 10.1007/s11222-013-9416-2 <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-013-9416-2>).

Could this be changed in the faq to either cite the paper or in some other way give reference to the article to make it findable?

Thanks in advance,
Kristian

messages.subject: Implementing a spatial shared component model in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Implementing a spatial shared component model in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am looking to implement a shared component model (SCM) in INLA, and have some questions about how to do so, and how the scaling factor is estimated.

A hypothetical example:

For each district (i = 1,2..n) and disease (d = 1,2), we have observed (O_di) and expected (E_di) counts.

I want to fit a straightforward SCM to estimate standardized mortality ratios, with bym2 parameterization for the shared and disease specific spatial effects

log(theta_{1i}) = alpha_{1} + phi_{i} / delta + psi_{1i}
log(theta_{2i}) = alpha_{2} + phi_{i} * delta + psi_{2i}

My approach in INLA:
data$obs = c(O_1i, O_2i) #O_1i is vector of observed counts for disease 1, etc.
data$exp = c(E_1i, E_2i)
data$district.id <http://district.id> = c(1:n, 1:n)
data$dis1 = c(rep(1, n), rep(0, n))
data$dis2 = c(rep(0, n), rep(1, n))
data$district.dis1.id <http://district.dis1.id> = c(1:n, rep(NA, n))
data$district.dis2.id <http://district.dis2.id> = c(rep(NA, n), 1:n)
data$district.dis1.id2 = c(1:n, rep(NA, n))
data$district.dis2.id2 = c(rep(NA, n), 1:n)

formula <- obs ~ -1 + dis1 + dis2 +
f(district.dis1.id <http://district.dis1.id>, model = "bym2", graph=g, scale.model=T, constr=T) +
f(district.dis2.id <http://district.dis2.id>, copy = "district.dis1.id <http://district.dis1.id>", fixed = FALSE, hyper = list(beta = list(prior = "normal", param = c(0, 1/tau_delta))), range = c(0, Inf)) +
f(district.dis1.id2, model = "bym2", graph=g, scale.model=T, constr=T) +
f(district.dis1.id2, model = "bym2", graph=g, scale.model=T, constr=T)

  mod<- inla(formula,
                family = "poisson",
                data = data,
                E = data$exp)

My understanding of the copy feature is INLA is that the above model would estimate a scaling factor by which the disease 2 county-specific random effects are multiplied, but the REs for disease 1 are not scaled. That is, in contrast to the equations above:

log(theta_{1i}) = alpha_{1} + phi_{i} + psi_{1i} (not scaled by 1/delta)
log(theta_{2i}) = alpha_{2} + phi_{i} * delta + psi_{2i}

Was wondering if I am understanding correctly, and if so, how would I estimate phi_{i} REs as expressed in the first set of equations, "inbetween" the scaled effects for each race.

Thank you!
Shu

messages.subject: Calculating Marginal Effects in INLA with GAM and Random Walks
messages.subject_clean: Calculating Marginal Effects in INLA with GAM and Random Walks
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I'm seeking guidance on calculating marginal effects in INLA when using Generalized Additive Models (GAM) with random walks (rw2). Specifically, I want to examine the impact of a 1.5K increase in global warming on disease incidence.

My usual approach is to hold all variables constant except the one of interest and make predictions. However, I'm unsure if this works in INLA with GAM and rw2. I've implemented a simulation study, but after reviewing a study by Gibb et al. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43954-0), I have doubts about my approach.

To briefly explain, I created two new datasets and added them to the initial one. I did this because INLA does not have a predict function for new datasets. I set Y as NA and, for the duplicate datasets, kept all variables constant at their mean, equal for all NUTS (my spatial unit), and for the population (given that it is an offset), I kept it constant as the mean per each NUTS across years. This copy was done to isolate the effect of temperature alone in the predictions.

For the effect on future temperature values I then created a future scenario dataset where I have all the same variables as above, but with the temperature increased by 1.5K. I then ran the model, calculated the predictions performed my analysis for the risk change using a linear model.

Gibb et al. used INLA to test for changes in temperature-driven dengue risk, but their code (https://github.com/rorygibb/dengue_vietnam_ms/blob/v1.0.0/scripts_full/05_analysis/10_analysis_temperatureproj_era5.R) seems to interpolate the risk function, which I don't fully understand.

My questions are:

Can I isolate the effect of one variable (temperature) by holding all other variables constant and making predictions, as I would in a traditional model framework when implementing a GAM with random walk2 in INLA? In case my approach is wrong, how can I deal with this question?

Attached a reproducible code you can run to understand what I did

Thank you
Angela

messages.subject: The inla result collection failed, when verbose = FALSE
messages.subject_clean: The inla result collection failed, when verbose = FALSE
messages.body_plain:
I have recently reinstalled INLA in order to get back to an old spatial modelling project I was working on 3 years ago.

I have been testing the installation, including using the test example given at https://www.r-inla.org/download-install

The issue I am having is that whenever I execute an inla() model, if verbose is set to FALSE (the default), the model fails with:
Error in inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts, : The inla result collection failed.

However if I set verbose to TRUE, then the model executes as expected. I have tried this with several different models and on two separate computer systems and this error consistently occurs. While not strictly a problem per se, it seems like an odd quirk of the inla() rather than e.g. problems with model specification. Test model code and session info provided below.

Best,
Mat :)

library(INLA)
n = 100; a = 1; b = 1; tau = 100
z = rnorm(n)
eta = a + b*z
scale = exp(rnorm(n))
prec = scale*tau
y = rnorm(n, mean = eta, sd = 1/sqrt(prec))
data = list(y=y, z=z)
formula = y ~ 1+z
result = inla(formula, family = "gaussian", data = data)

messages.subject: Detecting unstable precision estimates
messages.subject_clean: Detecting unstable precision estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm running simulations using INLA to fit phylogenetic models with one covariate and two random effects (species IID and phylogenetic using a correlation matrix). In approximately 2 per cent of runs, the model returns large random effect variance estimates >10 (e.g., either for species or phylo or for both), but without any convergence warnings. I’ve attached the model output and the code of one model with simulated data that shows a large variance estimate for the phylo random effect even though I have used a penalised complexity (PC) prior on the phylo effect.

To improve the estimates, I am thinking of:

·        Changing the prior to param = c(1, 0.1), given I simulated the variances of the random components to be lower than 1.

·        Adding a PC prior to the species random effect.

·        Centering the simulated covariate (mean = 0)

My question:
Are there built-in INLA diagnostics or object components (beyond `model_inla$ok` and `model_inla$mode$mode.status`) that I can query to automatically flag runs with unstable or extreme precision estimates? I’d like a single logical flag or numeric indicator in the fitted object for use in my simulation, without plotting or inspecting marginals manually.

Thank you in advance for your help and insights.

Coralie

Session info:

R 4.4.2

R-INLA 24.06.27

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm having this issue:
The problem is that the version of the inla.mkl executable installed by INLA was compiled with GLIBC 2.38 or higher, but my system (Ubuntu) has an older version (probably 2.35 or 2.36).

Thank you very much in advance
Miguel

> Dear Thierry
>
> I know this post has been dormant for awhile, but I'm having a similar issue. I'm fitting my model to air pollution ground measurement sites and predicting on the grid.
>
> I get how to add the IID site term, but how do you practically go about adding the additional variance to the posteriors?
>
> Would this be within the INLA fit and predict together call, added after this, or where you constructed the posterior predictive distributions manually using inla.posterior.sample?

> Any help on this would be great!

> > Dear Sylvan,
> >
> > You can assume that the idd models some noise at the locations (the nugget of the semi-variogram). It only affects the point estimate of a specific measurement at a given location. Another observation at the same location is likely to get a different idd effect. Hence for the prediction you don't use the individual estimates of the idd random effect. Instead you need to add the variance of the idd effect.
> >
> > model for location i: \eta_i = intercept + spde_i + iid_i
> >
> > predict while ignoring the iid effect \eta_i = intercept + spde_i This prediction has variance \sigma^2_e. You need to add the variance of the iid effect to get the correct posterior distribution.
> > \eta_i = N(mean = intercept + spde_i, variance = \sigma^2_e + \sigma^2_iid)

> > > Cheers,

> > > >

messages.subject: Why does inla.group.cv() return NA for some zero-inflated Poisson models?
messages.subject_clean: Why does inla.group.cv() return NA for some zero-inflated Poisson models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi ,
I'm working on evaluating the predictive performance of spatio-temporal models when the proportion of zeros in the data is high.

I've tested several models (Poisson, zeroinflatedpoisson1, and zeroinflatedpoisson0) each without and with an interaction (Type I).

According to the WAIC criterion, the best model is:

bym2.rw2.iid_intI_iid.base <- inla(formula.bym2.rw2.iid_intI_iid,
                                   family=family,data=map,E=E,verbose = TRUE,
                                   control.compute = control.compute, control.inla = control.inla)

Next, I attempted to implement the U(LGOCV) approach using the grouping structure from this selected model

gcpo.default.3.base <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(bym2.rw2.iid_intI_iid.base, num.level.sets = 3, strategy = "posterior")
gcpo.ZIP1.bym2..iid.base<- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(ZIP1.bym2..iid.base , group.cv <http://group.cv> = gcpo.default.3.base)
gcpo.ZIP0.bym2..iid.base<- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(ZIP0.bym2..iid.base , group.cv <http://group.cv> = gcpo.default.3.base)
gcpo.ZIP1.bym2.rw2.base<- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(ZIP1.bym2.rw2.base , group.cv <http://group.cv> = gcpo.default.3.base)
gcpo.ZIP0.bym2.rw2.base<- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(ZIP0.bym2.rw2.base , group.cv <http://group.cv> = gcpo.default.3.base)

------------------------------------ The problem  ------------------------------------

When computing U(LGOCV, I get:

-mean(log(gcpo.ZIP1.bym2..iid.base$cv)) returns  NA
-mean(log(gcpo.ZIP0.bym2..iid.base$cv)) returns  0.3774887

-mean(log(gcpo.ZIP1.bym2.rw2.base$cv)) returns NA
-mean(log(gcpo.ZIP0.bym2.rw2.base$cv)) returns  NA

I'm trying to understand why some of these cross-validation results return NA . Is it due to zero predictions, numerical issues, or something else related to the ZIP models or group structure?

------------------------------------ Model formulas ------------------------------------

formula.bym2.rw2.iid_intI_iid <- O ~
  f(ID, model = "bym2", graph = g_ePIMAD,hyper = hyper_bym,constr = T, scale.model = T)+
  f(Year_int,model="rw2",hyper = hyper_iid_rw,constr = T, scale.model = T)+
  f(Year_int_bis,model="iid",hyper = hyper_iid_rw,constr = T)+
  f(SPID.Year,model="iid",hyper = hyper_iid_rw,constr = T)

formula.bym2..iid <- O ~
  f(ID, model = "bym2", graph = g_ePIMAD,hyper = hyper_bym,constr = T, scale.model = T)+
  f(Year_int_bis,model="iid",hyper = hyper_iid_rw,constr = T)

ZIP1.bym2..iid.base <- inla(formula.bym2..iid,
                            family="zeroinflatedpoisson1",data=map,E=E,verbose = TRUE,
                            control.compute = control.compute, control.inla = control.inla)

ZIP0.bym2..iid.base <- inla(formula.bym2..iid,
                            family="zeroinflatedpoisson0",data=map,E=E,verbose = TRUE,
                            control.compute = control.compute,control.inla = control.inla)

formula.bym2.rw2 <- O ~
  f(ID, model = "bym2", graph = g_ePIMAD,hyper = hyper_bym,constr = T, scale.model = T)+
  f(Year_int,model="rw2",hyper = hyper_iid_rw,constr = T, scale.model = T)

ZIP1.bym2.rw2.base <- inla(formula.bym2.rw2,
                           family="zeroinflatedpoisson1",data=map,E=E,verbose = TRUE,
                           control.compute = control.compute, control.inla = control.inla)

  Thanks in advance for any help or suggestions!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
There are several ways of doing this; if you run the model with inlabru and use mapper=bru_mapper_index(nr_individual_values), then generate() and predict() will generate new numbers for the iid effect in the posterior sampling for indices above the max-index in the estimation, and you can compute whatever quantity you want (except spatial integrals, as iid noise is not integrable)
If you just want to compute prediction scores and/or moments, then take a look at the examples on
Prediction scores <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#normal-model-example>
inlabru-org.github.io <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#normal-model-example>
 <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#normal-model-example>
There, the Normal example extracts the precision parameter for an iid effect (in that case just the one from the observation model) and incorporates that into the calculations.
Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Detecting unstable precision estimates
messages.body_plain:
its plausible to think that gaussian data is the most easiest case, but its not.
the unknown scale of the data makes this (and similar) likelihood sensitive to
non-centering issues, and secondly, also initial values. its almost impossible
to write code that cannot be broken by scaling and offset data and covariates.
also the posterior *is* multimodal, as several interpreations of the data
exists.

in your case, then centering of covariate 'x' will help. this just shift the
burden onto the intercept, which is 'centered' using a fixed offset. for the
'random effect' I would suggest adding constr=T to center them, as your priors
is pretty vague, which implicite suggest that you allow them to fly away from
zero.

I would guess this formula will be pretty stable. if you run into issues, then
can fix a higher initial values for 'iid' and 'generic0' adding

hyper = list(prec=list(initial=8)))

so that its higher than the initial value for the likelihood (which 4, which can
be lowered if you know roughtly the scale)

let me know how this goes

best
H

dat$x <- dat$x - mean(dat$x)
dat$off <- mean(dat$y)
model_inla <- inla(yi ~ offset(off) + x + f(species,
                                        #hyper = pcprior,
                              model = "iid",
                              constr = TRUE) +
                       f(phylo, ## this needs to be a numeric to work
                         model = "generic0",
                         constr = TRUE,
                         hyper=pcprior,
                         Cmatrix = phylo.prec.mat),
                   family = "gaussian",
                   data = dat)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if you've managed to get the predictions on the mesh nodes, then fm_evaluate/or method/s (inla.mesh.project/or are deprecated) can be used to interpolate,
with something like
  fm_evaluate(mesh, loc = fm_pixels(mesh, mask = polygon_boundary_for_region_of_interest, format = "sf"), field = values_at_all_the_mesh_nodes)
or you can directly call inlabru::g() to do that calculation for you, if all you want to do is visualise:
  ggplot() + gg(data = mesh, col = values_at_all_the_mesh_nodes, mask = polygon_boundary_...)
(see ?inlabru::gg.fm_mesh_2d )
In both cases, the `mask` argument is optional, and is used to only show values inside a region of interest.

If your inla output gives you a vector that contains the values for each vertex, but for each multinomial alternative, you'll need to extract the relevant subset of the vector. The indexing order should be either (1:n, 1:n, ...), or (1, 1, 1, ..., 2, 2, 2, ...), so either
  [seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) + fm_dof(mesh) * (alternative - 1)]
or
  [alternative + num_alternatives * (seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) - 1)]

Finn

Many thanks, Finn.

I did what you told me, but something's still wrong.

I implemented the loop to fit the multinomial Poisson-trick model separately for each alternative. Fitting the model separately for each choice allowed me to extract predicted values independently for each alternative.

After obtaining these linear predictors, I extracted them and applied the softmax function to convert them into probabilities that sum to one across all alternatives, for every single location. As I understand, this step is essential to ensures that the predicted probabilities for all choices at a specific cell are properly scaled.

Regarding the predictions on the mesh nodes, I believe I managed to extract them correctly, but I'm not completely certain. Specifically, to retrieve the relevant subset of the prediction vector, I used indexing of the form:

alt + num_alternatives * (seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) - 1)

However, when I compared this indexing with:

seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) + fm_dof(mesh) * (alt - 1)

I obtained different sets of indices.

I have generated interpolations using fm_evaluate, but I am unsure whether these are correct. When I use inlabru::g() to visualize the results, I observe different behaviors depending on the indexing scheme. With the first indexing formula, I get values for only some triangles across all alternatives, and so many NA’s. With the second indexing formula, I get a range of values covering the entire area, but only for the first alternative. For alternatives 2 and 3, I obtain no values at all locations. I'm doing this wrong.

Finally, I then rasterized these predicted probabilities to produce regular spatial grids for each alternative. This enabled a structured and consistent visualization of the spatial distribution of predicted choice probabilities across the study area.

I’m attaching the script with the original implementation, focused only on the continuous spatial random effect, in case you can help me.

Many thanks

Miguel

messages.body_plain:
I don't know what you mean by estimating separately for each alternative. That sounds like a collection of Binary observation models, and not a Multinomial model.

If you change the fitting procedure, you also most likely changed the required indexing, since it likely means you changed the size of the model. Can you please focus on one implementation, and not change everything at once?

The two indexings are different, yes, and only one of them is correct. Once one figures out which one is correct, that's the one to use.
Both versions assume you've estimated the full model.

Finn

On Mon, 30 Jun 2025 at 02:53, Miguel Angel Salinas Melgoza <miguel....@umich.mx> wrote:

> Many thanks, Finn.
>
> I did what you told me, but something's still wrong.
>
> I implemented the loop to fit the multinomial Poisson-trick model separately for each alternative. Fitting the model separately for each choice allowed me to extract predicted values independently for each alternative.
>
> After obtaining these linear predictors, I extracted them and applied the softmax function to convert them into probabilities that sum to one across all alternatives, for every single location. As I understand, this step is essential to ensures that the predicted probabilities for all choices at a specific cell are properly scaled.
>
> Regarding the predictions on the mesh nodes, I believe I managed to extract them correctly, but I'm not completely certain. Specifically, to retrieve the relevant subset of the prediction vector, I used indexing of the form:
>
> alt + num_alternatives * (seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) - 1)
>
> However, when I compared this indexing with:
>
> seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) + fm_dof(mesh) * (alt - 1)
>
> I obtained different sets of indices.
>
> I have generated interpolations using fm_evaluate, but I am unsure whether these are correct. When I use inlabru::g() to visualize the results, I observe different behaviors depending on the indexing scheme. With the first indexing formula, I get values for only some triangles across all alternatives, and so many NA’s. With the second indexing formula, I get a range of values covering the entire area, but only for the first alternative. For alternatives 2 and 3, I obtain no values at all locations. I'm doing this wrong.
>
> Finally, I then rasterized these predicted probabilities to produce regular spatial grids for each alternative. This enabled a structured and consistent visualization of the spatial distribution of predicted choice probabilities across the study area.
>
> I’m attaching the script with the original implementation, focused only on the continuous spatial random effect, in case you can help me.
>
> Many thanks
>
> Miguel
>
> El viernes, 27 de junio de 2025 a las 1:47:31 UTC-6, Finn Lindgren escribió:
> > Hi,
> >
> > if you've managed to get the predictions on the mesh nodes, then fm_evaluate/or method/s (inla.mesh.project/or are deprecated) can be used to interpolate,
> > with something like
> >   fm_evaluate(mesh, loc = fm_pixels(mesh, mask = polygon_boundary_for_region_of_interest, format = "sf"), field = values_at_all_the_mesh_nodes)
> > or you can directly call inlabru::g() to do that calculation for you, if all you want to do is visualise:
> >   ggplot() + gg(data = mesh, col = values_at_all_the_mesh_nodes, mask = polygon_boundary_...)
> > (see ?inlabru::gg.fm_mesh_2d )
> > In both cases, the `mask` argument is optional, and is used to only show values inside a region of interest.
> >
> > If your inla output gives you a vector that contains the values for each vertex, but for each multinomial alternative, you'll need to extract the relevant subset of the vector. The indexing order should be either (1:n, 1:n, ...), or (1, 1, 1, ..., 2, 2, 2, ...), so either
> >   [seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) + fm_dof(mesh) * (alternative - 1)]
> > or
> >   [alternative + num_alternatives * (seq_len(fm_dof(mesh)) - 1)]
